GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus:
Overview — The Muscular Conduit

The oesophagus is a ~25 cm muscular tube carrying food from the pharynx to the stomach. It has no digestive or absorptive role — it is built for abrasion resistance (a tough stratified squamous lining) and propulsion (peristalsis).

🔬 Image slot — oesophagus at low power — folded (star-shaped) lumen, the four concentric layers, and submucosal glands

It follows the general four-layer plan of the GI tract, and every hollow gut organ is read the same way — from lumen outward:

1
Mucosaepithelium + lamina propria + muscularis mucosae
2
Submucosadense CT, vessels, glands, Meissner plexus
3
Muscularis externainner circular + outer longitudinal, Auerbach plexus
4
Adventitia / serosaouter wrapping
Two features let you name the oesophagus at a glance: a non-keratinised stratified squamous lining and mucous glands sitting in the submucosa. Together they are almost unique to the oesophagus.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — oesophageal wall — thick stratified squamous epithelium, lamina propria, thick muscularis mucosae, submucosal mucous glands
  • Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium — thick, pale, with flattened surface cells that keep their nuclei (no keratin layer).
  • Folded, star-shaped lumen — longitudinal mucosal/submucosal folds that flatten out when a bolus passes.
  • Oesophageal glands proper in the submucosa — the single best discriminator (few other places have submucosal mucous glands; the duodenum's Brunner glands are the other classic).
  • Thick muscularis mucosae of mostly longitudinal smooth muscle — unusually prominent here.
  • Adventitia, not serosa, over most of its length (it is a retroperitoneal/mediastinal tube).
Stratified squamous lumen + mucous glands in the submucosa → oesophagus. If instead you see squamous epithelium with no submucosal glands, think vagina/anal canal; if you see it keratinised, think skin.
Layer 1 — Mucosa
🔬 Image slot — oesophageal mucosa — stratified squamous epithelium, lamina propria papillae, muscularis mucosae
Epithelium
  • Non-keratinised stratified squamous — protects against mechanical abrasion from food
  • Continuously renewed from a basal layer; surface cells retain nuclei
Lamina propria
  • Loose CT with vessels & immune cells
  • Contains oesophageal cardiac glands near the two ends (mucous; protect against reflux/abrasion)
  • Muscularis mucosae — here it is thick and mostly longitudinal (a useful clue); it thickens distally toward the stomach.
Two named mucous glands — don’t mix them up: cardiac glands lie in the lamina propria at the ends; glands proper lie in the submucosa along the whole length.
Layer 2 — Submucosa & the Oesophageal Glands
🔬 Image slot — submucosa — tubuloacinar mucous glands (oesophageal glands proper) with ducts crossing the muscularis mucosae, plus a venous plexus
  • Dense irregular connective tissue carrying the larger blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves.
  • Oesophageal glands proper — small tubuloacinar mucous glands scattered along the whole length; their ducts pierce the mucosa to lubricate the bolus.
  • Meissner (submucosal) plexus — autonomic ganglia controlling glandular secretion and local blood flow.
  • A longitudinal submucosal venous plexus — clinically vital (see varices below).
The distal oesophageal submucosal veins are a porto-systemic anastomosis (left gastric vein → azygos). In portal hypertension they dilate into oesophageal varices — a lethal cause of upper-GI bleeding.
Layer 3 — Muscularis Externa (the “Two-Thirds” Rule)
🔬 Image slot — muscularis externa — inner circular and outer longitudinal layers with the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between them

Two layers — inner circular and outer longitudinal — but the muscle type changes down the length, which is a favourite exam point:

↑
Upper 1/3Skeletal (striated) muscle — voluntary start of swallowing
↔
Middle 1/3Mixed skeletal + smooth muscle
↓
Lower 1/3Smooth muscle — involuntary peristalsis
  • Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between the two muscle layers and drives peristalsis.
  • Upper & lower oesophageal sphincters bracket the tube: the UOS (cricopharyngeus) is skeletal; the LOS is a physiological smooth-muscle sphincter reinforced by the diaphragmatic crura.
Loss of the myenteric ganglion cells in the lower oesophagus → the LOS fails to relax and peristalsis is lost → achalasia (a “bird’s-beak” tapering on barium swallow).
Layer 4 — Adventitia vs Serosa
  • Most of the oesophagus is in the neck/thorax and is wrapped by adventitia — connective tissue that blends into surrounding mediastinal structures (no mesothelial covering).
  • Only the short abdominal segment (below the diaphragm) has a true serosa (mesothelium).
Because most of the wall lacks a serosal barrier, oesophageal tumours spread locally early and perforations leak into the mediastinum — part of why oesophageal cancer carries a poor prognosis.
The Gastro-oesophageal Junction & Barrett’s
🔬 Image slot — gastro-oesophageal junction — abrupt Z-line where stratified squamous meets gastric simple columnar epithelium
  • At the gastro-oesophageal junction the lining changes abruptly from stratified squamous to the simple columnar epithelium of the gastric cardia — the Z-line (squamocolumnar junction).
  • Barrett’s oesophagus = chronic acid reflux drives metaplasia of the squamous lining into columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).
Barrett’s is premalignant — it is the key risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma, so it is monitored by surveillance endoscopy & biopsy for dysplasia.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Reflux oesophagitis (GORD)
Basal cell hyperplasia, elongated lamina-propria papillae, and intra-epithelial eosinophils/neutrophils
Barrett’s oesophagus
Squamous → columnar + goblet-cell (intestinal) metaplasia; premalignant
Adenocarcinoma
Lower third; arises from Barrett’s; risk = GORD, obesity — commonest type in the West
Squamous cell carcinoma
Upper/middle third; risk = smoking & alcohol — commonest type worldwide
Oesophageal varices
Dilated submucosal veins in portal hypertension → catastrophic upper-GI bleed
Achalasia
Loss of myenteric plexus ganglion cells → non-relaxing LOS & failed peristalsis
Eosinophilic oesophagitis
Allergic; >15 eosinophils/hpf, rings & furrows; dysphagia in young atopic patients
Mallory–Weiss tear
Mucosal laceration at the GOJ after forceful vomiting → haematemesis
⭐ Exam Pearls
Non-keratinised stratified squamous + submucosal mucous glands = oesophagus.
Four layers, read lumen-outward: mucosa → submucosa → muscularis externa → adventitia.
Muscularis externa muscle type: upper 1/3 skeletal, middle mixed, lower 1/3 smooth.
Glands proper = submucosa, whole length (lubrication); cardiac glands = lamina propria, at the two ends.
Auerbach (myenteric) plexus lies between the muscle layers (peristalsis); Meissner (submucosal) plexus controls glands/secretion.
Adventitia, not serosa, over most of its length → early local spread of tumours.
Z-line = abrupt squamous→columnar junction; Barrett’s = squamous→columnar+goblet metaplasia → adenocarcinoma.
SCC = upper/middle, smoking & alcohol; adenocarcinoma = lower third, Barrett’s/GORD.
Varices = submucosal veins in portal hypertension; achalasia = loss of myenteric ganglion cells.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (layers, gland:
Overview — The Acid-Secreting Mixing Sac

The stomach mixes food, secretes acid and enzymes, and begins protein digestion, turning the bolus into chyme. It keeps the four-layer GI plan but with three signature modifications: a simple columnar lining dipping into gastric pits, an extra (oblique) muscle layer, and mucosal folds called rugae.

🔬 Image slot — stomach at low power — simple columnar surface dipping into gastric pits, glands filling the mucosa, three muscle layers

It has four regions, and their glands differ — a favourite exam theme:

Cardia & Pylorus (antrum)
  • Deep pits, short coiled mucous glands
  • Pylorus is rich in G cells (gastrin)
Fundus & Body
  • Oxyntic (gastric) glands — the workhorse
  • Contain parietal + chief cells → acid & pepsinogen
Read the stomach in two steps: confirm it is stomach (columnar + pits, no goblet cells, no villi), then decide the region by which cells fill the glands.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — gastric mucosa — surface mucous cells, gastric pits, and glands packed with pink parietal and blue chief cells
  • Simple columnar surface epithelium that dips into gastric pits (foveolae) — the glands open at the pit base.
  • No goblet cells and no villi — this separates stomach from intestine at a glance.
  • In body/fundus: glands packed with pink (eosinophilic) parietal cells and blue (basophilic) chief cells.
  • In antrum/pylorus: deep pits over short, coiled, pale mucous glands (few/no parietal cells).
Columnar epithelium + gastric pits, but no goblet cells and no villi → stomach. The moment you see goblet cells or villi you are in intestine (or looking at intestinal metaplasia).
The Pit–Gland Unit
🔬 Image slot — the gastric pit-gland unit — pit (foveola), isthmus, neck (stem cells), and gland base

Each functional unit runs surface → base:

1
Gastric pit (foveola)lined by surface mucous cells
2
Isthmus / neckstem cells + mucous neck cells
3
Gland (body & base)parietal, chief & enteroendocrine cells
  • The pit : gland ratio maps region: deep pits/short glands in cardia & pylorus; short pits/long glands in body & fundus.
  • Stem cells in the isthmus/neck renew the epithelium — upward into the pit and downward into the gland.
The Five Cell Types (High-Yield)
Surface & neck mucous cells
Secrete bicarbonate-rich mucus that protects the lining; neck cells sit in the stem-cell zone
Parietal (oxyntic) cells
Pink/eosinophilic, “fried-egg”, central nucleus; secrete HCl (H⁺/K⁺ ATPase) & intrinsic factor; upper/mid gland
Chief (zymogenic) cells
Blue/basophilic base (RER) + apical zymogen granules; secrete pepsinogen & gastric lipase; gland base
Enteroendocrine cells
G cells (gastrin, antrum), ECL cells (histamine), D cells (somatostatin); at the gland base
Stem cells
In the isthmus/neck; renew all gastric epithelial cells
Parietal = Pink
  • Acid (HCl) + intrinsic factor
  • Round, central nucleus, canaliculi
  • Higher up the gland
Chief = Blue
  • Pepsinogen (→ pepsin in acid)
  • Basophilic basal cytoplasm
  • Deep at the gland base
Parietal Pink, Chief Chromatic-blue. Parietal cells make the two P’s — Proton (acid) and Protein-binder for B12 (intrinsic factor).
Acid Secretion & Its Control
🔬 Image slot — parietal cell — canaliculi, H+/K+ ATPase proton pump, and the gastrin / histamine / ACh inputs
  • The H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (proton pump) on the parietal-cell canaliculi pumps out H⁺ — the final common step and the target of PPIs.
  • Stimulate acid: gastrin (G cells), histamine (ECL cells, via H₂ receptors), ACh (vagus).
  • Inhibit acid: somatostatin (D cells); low pH switches off gastrin (negative feedback).
  • Intrinsic factor from parietal cells binds B12 for absorption in the terminal ileum.
Drug targets follow the biology: PPIs block the proton pump; H₂-blockers (ranitidine-type) block the histamine input; loss of parietal cells removes both acid and intrinsic factor.
Mucosal Barrier & the Extra Muscle Layer
Gastric mucosal barrier
  • Mucus–bicarbonate layer + surface tight junctions
  • Prostaglandins maintain mucus & blood flow
  • Rapid epithelial turnover
Muscularis externa
  • Three layers: inner oblique, middle circular, outer longitudinal
  • The extra oblique layer enables churning
  • Circular layer thickens at the pyloric sphincter
NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis → a weakened mucus/bicarbonate barrier → erosions and peptic ulcers.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
H. pylori gastritis
Curved bacilli in the antral mucus layer; causes chronic gastritis, ulcers, MALT lymphoma & adenocarcinoma
Peptic ulcer disease
Mucosal breach (H. pylori / NSAIDs); duodenal > gastric; risk of bleeding & perforation
Autoimmune (atrophic) gastritis
Anti-parietal & anti-IF antibodies → loss of parietal cells → achlorhydria + pernicious anaemia (B12); body/fundus
Intestinal metaplasia
Goblet cells appear in gastric mucosa → a premalignant change toward adenocarcinoma
Gastric adenocarcinoma
Intestinal type (glands, on metaplasia) vs diffuse type (signet-ring cells, linitis plastica, CDH1/E-cadherin loss)
Zollinger–Ellison
Gastrinoma → parietal-cell hyperplasia, high acid & refractory/multiple ulcers
Gastric MALT lymphoma
H. pylori-driven B-cell lymphoma; may regress with eradication
GIST
Mesenchymal tumour of the interstitial cells of Cajal; c-KIT (CD117) positive
⭐ Exam Pearls
Simple columnar + gastric pits, no goblet cells, no villi = stomach.
Parietal Pink (HCl + intrinsic factor, upper gland); Chief blue (pepsinogen, gland base).
Body/fundus = oxyntic glands (parietal + chief); antrum = G cells making gastrin.
H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (proton pump) = PPI target; acid driven by gastrin, histamine (ECL) & ACh, inhibited by somatostatin (D cells).
Stomach has three muscle layers (extra inner oblique) for churning.
Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia).
H. pylori → antral gastritis, peptic ulcers, MALT lymphoma & adenocarcinoma.
Intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells in stomach) is premalignant; diffuse carcinoma = signet-ring cells & linitis plastica.
NSAIDs block prostaglandins → weakened mucus/bicarbonate barrier → ulcers.
